opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It felt natural mostly because of the kind of work I wanted to be doing.

At Apollo, a lot of my focus was on fundamental interpretability research: trying to find better ways to decompose neural networks into parts we can actually understand. That work was, and is, important, but I kept running into the same thought: if these methods are going to matter, they need to be pushed hard against real models, at scale, and turned into tools people actually use. That's a different kind of pressure from writing a paper.

Goodfire's whole bet is that interpretability can be more than a scientific curiosity. It can be something you build on, something that helps you understand, debug, and eventually design models. That aligns closely with what I care about. I've always thought the long-term goal of interpretability isn't just to look inside models after the fact, but to give us real levers over what they're doing and why.

There's also a practical side. Goodfire has invested in the compute, the engineering, and the people to run ambitious research programs on large models, and to iterate quickly. For the parameter decomposition work and related ideas I'd been developing, that environment is valuable. You can ask bigger questions and find out faster whether your ideas hold up.

And honestly, the team was a big part of it. A lot of people there share the conviction that we're still early in understanding what's going on inside these systems, and that getting it right matters a great deal, both for safety and for making AI more useful and trustworthy. So it didn't feel like leaving one mission for another. It felt like continuing the same mission in a place set up to push it further.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Apollo’s fundamental interpretability work with Lee’s interest in applying it at scale, but does not say Apollo shifted toward evaluations or that this reduced the fit for his team.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that the research agenda didn't really change, the context around it did. At Apollo, a lot of what I'd been working on was this question of how do you decompose a network into the parts that actually matter for its computation, things like attribution-based parameter decomposition and the stuff that came before it. And that's fundamentally a question about what the right units of analysis are inside a model. That's not a question you can really answer by only thinking about safety. It's a question about the science of these systems.

And Goodfire is, I think, one of the few places that's taking that seriously as an engineering problem and not just a research curiosity. They're building the infrastructure to actually apply interpretability at scale, on real models, with real users who care whether the method works. And for me that's quite important, because one of the failure modes of interpretability as a field is that you can produce very pretty pictures of toy models and never find out whether any of it generalizes. Having a feedback loop where the methods get pressure-tested against models people are actually deploying is a pretty good forcing function.

The other thing is that I came to feel that the distinction between "safety interpretability" and "interpretability that's useful for other things" is somewhat artificial. If you can genuinely understand what a model is doing, that's useful for steering it, for debugging it, for catching deceptive behavior, for making it more reliable. The same underlying understanding serves all of those. So working somewhere that's trying to make interpretability actually useful, rather than treating it as a purely academic exercise, didn't feel like a departure from the safety motivation at all. It felt like the thing you'd do if you took the safety motivation seriously and wanted the methods to actually be ready when they're needed.

And honestly, part of it was just that there's a group of people there I wanted to work with, and the culture seemed like one where the fundamental research and the applied work could feed each other rather than competing for attention. That's rarer than it should be.

astra-6.text:
For me, the common thread was interpretability. At Apollo, I was interested in how we could understand what’s going on inside models well enough to tell whether they’re doing something concerning, rather than just relying on their outputs. And that naturally leads to the question: if we can understand those internal mechanisms, can we also change them?

That’s what made Goodfire feel like a natural fit. It was an opportunity to make interpretability practically useful—to use that understanding to steer models and improve their behavior. I see those as closely connected goals: understanding models so we can assess them, and understanding models so we can have more control over them.
